Chapter 11: Judgment, Prejudice, and the Courage to Change One’s Mind
We all carry judgments with us—about people, ideas, even ourselves. Some of these come from family or culture, and others are shaped by our own experiences. Most of the time, we hardly notice them. They quietly guide our choices and shape our opinions without us even realizing. But every now and then, something happens that challenges what we think we know. Suddenly, there’s a chance to change.
Montaigne really understood just how dangerous prejudice can be. He saw how quick we are to judge others—sometimes just by their appearance, background, or even rumors we’ve heard. And he also knew how tough it can be to let go of those judgments, even when the facts tell a different story.
Imagine this: someone has always believed that a certain group of people just can’t be trusted. But one day, they have to work closely with someone from that group. At first, there’s suspicion—the old judgment lingers. But as they spend time together, something shifts. Respect grows, and maybe even friendship. That old belief? It starts to fall apart, replaced by real understanding.
Here’s something important to remember: changing your mind doesn’t mean you’re weak. In fact, it takes real strength and courage to admit when a belief isn’t right, or when it’s time for a fresh perspective. Most of us are uncomfortable with uncertainty, but if you can face it, you’ll find a kind of freedom you might not expect.
Picture a leader who’s spent years insisting on one policy, no matter what. One day, this leader actually listens to the people affected by those decisions. Their stories make an impact. Slowly, a new approach takes shape. Of course, it’s not easy—there’s pushback and criticism. But the leader stands firm, knowing deep down that this change is the right thing to do.
Now, judgment itself isn’t always a bad thing. We need it to make decisions, protect ourselves, and find our way in the world. But when judgment hardens into prejudice, it closes us off—it shuts down our minds and our hearts. The real challenge? Staying open. It’s about questioning your own assumptions, seeking out new experiences, and really listening to people who see things differently.
It’s natural to resist change, to hold on to beliefs that feel safe and familiar. But life is unpredictable, and wisdom comes from being able to adapt. By letting go of rigid judgments, you open yourself up to growth, connection, and a much deeper sense of compassion for others.
